Hays Area Bee Garden Guide

A gardener-friendly bee and plant interaction guide for Hays County and the broader Central Texas area. Use the plant guide to decide what to plant, and the bee checklist to explore which bees may use those plants.

213species-level bee names
209plant taxa linked to bees

Start here: use this like a garden guide

1. Start with plants.
Most gardeners need to know what to plant first. The plant guide ranks plants by how many bee taxa they are linked to in the dataset.
2. Prefer local support.
Hays-core and near-Kyle records are stronger for local decisions than broad regional or uncertain records.
3. Read counts carefully.
A high count means more source-backed dataset rows, not more individual bees in your yard.
4. Verify before planting.
Check native status, water need, bloom season, and site fit before using a plant in a conservation planting.

Plain-language rule: use this page to find good leads, then verify the plant with local native-plant references before buying seed or installing it.

How to read the data

Count meaning

Unique plants means different plant taxa recorded with a bee. Source-backed rows means workbook evidence rows with source/citation fields. It is not a count of individual bees.

Direct visit/feeding rows are stronger garden clues than broad interactsWith rows.

Family-level nesting clues

  • Andrenidae: Many are solitary ground-nesters. Keep some sunny bare soil and avoid sealing every patch with mulch.
  • Apidae: Very mixed family. Some nest in soil, wood, stems, cavities, or colonies. Use season-long bloom diversity.
  • Megachilidae: Many use hollow stems, cavities, mud, leaf pieces, resin, or plant fibers. Leave stems and avoid over-cleaning.
  • Halictidae: Many are small ground-nesting bees. Bare soil patches and low-disturbance edges can matter.
  • Colletidae: Many line nest cells with a waterproof material; several nest in soil or stems. Avoid over-managing every nesting edge.

Interaction legend

Flower visitvisitsFlowersOf

The bee is recorded visiting the flower. This is the clearest garden-use signal in this dataset.

Visitvisits

A visit was recorded, but the dataset term is less specific than visitsFlowersOf.

Feeding recordeats

A feeding relationship was recorded. Direction matters in the original evidence row.

General associationinteractsWith

The dataset records an association, but not a precise behavior. Treat as a lead, not proof of flower use.

Nearby recordadjacentTo

Nearby/co-occurrence evidence. Weak for plant-choice decisions.

Parasite relationshipparasiteOf

Parasitism/host relationship. Useful for ecology, not a planting recommendation by itself.

Internal parasite relationshipendoparasiteOf

Internal parasitism/host relationship. Useful for ecology, not a planting recommendation by itself.

Host relationshiphasHost

Host relationship. Direction matters in the original evidence row.

Predator/preypreysOn

Predator/prey relationship. Useful for ecology, not a planting recommendation by itself.

Local confidence legend

Hays-core locality text

The locality text mentions a Hays-area place. Good local lead, but still check the source row.

≤25 mi / ≤50 mi from Kyle

Coordinates are close to Kyle. Useful for Hays-area gardening and restoration decisions.

≤150 mi from Kyle

Regional Central Texas / surrounding-area evidence. Useful, but weaker than Hays or near-Kyle records.

uncertain/outside

Retained for audit. Do not use alone as a planting recommendation.

Important caveat

A source-backed interaction is a dataset record, not always a photo-vouchered Hays County plant visit. Use it like a map of clues, not a final proof list.
